section_summary: This final section documents Japanese Army propaganda, internal factional conflict, and expanding influence over foreign policy during 1935–1936. It includes a War Department pamphlet portraying the Soviet Union and United States as threats, reports on the assassination of General Tetsuzan Nagata and the struggle between moderate and radical Army factions, and observations from Japanese-occupied Manchuria. The closing documents concern command changes in North China and Japanese Army casualties in Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Why General Nagata Died
subfiles.about: A German newspaper analyzes the political and social outlook of the Japanese officer movement associated with Nagata’s assassin.
subfiles.summary: Article describes the officer movement as authoritarian, anticapitalist and nationalist, linked to poor soldiers and peasants and seeking total mobilization of society.

subfiles.title: Review of the Japanese War Department Pamphlet on the International Situation
subfiles.about: An internal review summarizes the arguments and political purpose of the Japanese Army’s September 5 pamphlet.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum judges that the pamphlet was intended to sustain public alarm and facilitate military appropriations. It identifies the Soviet Union as the principal alleged enemy and the United States as the second, while highlighting the pamphlet’s demand for redistribution of territory and natural resources according to population.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1466: Japanese Army Pamphlet of September 5, 1935
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Neville transmits and evaluates a Japanese War Department propaganda pamphlet issued for popular consumption.
subfiles.summary: Neville reports 100,000 copies of an Army pamphlet printed September 5, 1935, to maintain support for military preparations, casting the USSR and US as enemies and demanding territorial redistribution.

subfiles.title: Japan and the Period of Change in the International Situation
subfiles.about: A Japanese Army pamphlet argues that international inequality and foreign threats require military expansion and a Japanese-led restructuring of East Asia.
subfiles.summary: The pamphlet depicts world conflict as the product of unequal access to territory, raw materials, markets, and migration and calls for their redistribution in favor of populous, resource-poor states such as Japan. It portrays the Soviet Union as a heavily armed and expansionist threat in Manchuria and the United States as a naval and diplomatic obstacle to Japanese continental policy. China is described as divided, vulnerable to communism, and in need of Japanese guidance, while Manchukuo is presented as the foundation for an allegedly moral and peaceful regional order. The tract concludes that Japan must strengthen its armed forces and assume leadership of Asia.

subfiles.title: Departmental Note on Tokyo Despatch No. 1455
subfiles.about: An internal note evaluates the Embassy’s report on the aftermath of Nagata’s assassination and the appointment of Kawashima.
subfiles.summary: Note: Despatch No. 1455 adds little to the attaché report; Kawashima will probably continue Hayashi's reform and unification, with no political repercussions expected.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1455: Aftermath of the Assassination of General Nagata
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Embassy reports Hayashi’s response to Nagata’s assassination, his Army-control program, and his replacement by Kawashima.
subfiles.summary: Hayashi temporarily remained Minister of War to issue instructions strengthening discipline, suppressing cliques and rumors, limiting officers’ political contacts, and improving relations between central and provincial commands. The Embassy attributes Aizawa’s attack to both personal resentment and ideological hostility toward Nagata’s industrial-preparedness policies. After inaugurating his reforms, Hayashi resigned and was succeeded by Yoshiyuki Kawashima, a conservative officer expected to continue the same policies. The despatch concludes that the more conservative Army element would probably remain in control.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 1475
subfiles.about: A file note directs researchers to a political report concerning Nagata’s assassination and Hayashi’s Army-unification program.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 1475 (894.00 P.R./93): Nagata's assassination by Aizawa and Hayashi's Army unification program.

subfiles.title: Abstract on Nagata’s Assassination and Hayashi’s Program
subfiles.about: A brief abstract describes Aizawa’s motives and Hayashi’s decision to remain temporarily as Minister of War.
subfiles.summary: Aizawa probably held a personal grievance over his Taiwan assignment but turned it into a patriotic attack; Hayashi did not resign immediately and reiterated his unification program.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 1515
subfiles.about: A file note points to a political report on Hayashi’s resignation and Kawashima’s appointment.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 1515 (894.00 P.R./94): General Kawashima replaces War Minister Hayashi.

subfiles.title: The Army: Ministerial Changes, the Vice Minister, and the September 5 Pamphlet
subfiles.about: An Embassy report summarizes senior War Ministry changes and the themes of the September Army pamphlet.
subfiles.summary: Extract: Hayashi's delayed resignation, Kawashima's succession, Furusho as Vice Minister, Hashimoto's refusal of a division, and the September 5 pamphlet as propaganda naming the USSR and US enemies.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for the Secretary on Disunity in the Japanese Army
subfiles.about: An internal memorandum recommends Salisbury’s analysis of Japanese Army factions and its implications for policy toward China.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum explains Salisbury’s background and emphasizes the value of his civilian Japanese sources. It contrasts the earlier moderate Ugaki period with the contemporary dominance of the nationalist Araki–Masaki faction and concludes that no immediate moderation of Japanese military policy toward China should be expected.

subfiles.title: Despatch Forwarding Memoranda on the Japanese Army and Manchukuo
subfiles.from: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Embassy, Shanghai
subfiles.about: Johnson forwards two memoranda by Laurence Salisbury on Japanese Army disunity and conditions in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The despatch states that Salisbury’s Army information came from conversations held in Tokyo with Japanese civilians and officials between October 11 and 17. It also encloses his impressions of Manchuria from a train journey between Beijing and Japan.

subfiles.title: Disunity in the Japanese Army
subfiles.about: Salisbury analyzes the moderate and radical factions within the Japanese Army and their political significance.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum distinguishes a moderate Hayashi–Imai group from the stronger radical Araki–Masaki faction, while also discussing Ugaki, Minami, and officers stationed in China. Civilian informants allege that the radicals knew beforehand of Nagata’s assassination and intended it to intimidate the moderates. Although moderate influence and public doubts about the military were reportedly growing, no early change in the Army’s North China policy was expected. The informants also believed Western opposition after the Manchurian Incident had strengthened the Japanese military domestically.

subfiles.title: Conditions in Manchukuo as Seen on a Trip from Shanhaiguan to Dandong
subfiles.about: Salisbury records impressions of Japanese occupation and colonial society during a railway journey across Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Salisbury travels from Shanhaiguan to Dandong: Coppin's pro-Japanese propaganda, Japanese settlers dominating, uneasy foreigners in Mukden, and bandit precautions.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet on the Military’s Position in Japanese Politics
subfiles.about: A file note points to a later despatch containing a Dickover–Kurusu conversation about military influence in Japanese politics.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 1645 (894.00/561): Dickover-Kurusu conversation on the Japanese military's political position.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet on Forthcoming Japanese Army Changes
subfiles.about: A file note identifies a China telegram reporting Japanese Army command changes expected in March.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Lockhart report on Japanese Army changes announced by the Tokyo Asahi (793.94/7749).

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 89 on Japanese Command Changes in North China
subfiles.about: A telegram reports prospective changes in Japanese Army commands and their implications for the North China Garrison.
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 89: Tashiro to replace Tada in North China, with Kita as chief of staff, and Matsumuro to replace Doihara at Mukden; the changes foreshadow a stronger garrison.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet on Japanese Army Casualties in Manchuria
subfiles.about: A file note points to a Mukden political report on Japanese Army casualties in Manchuria during 1935.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Mukden report on Japanese Army casualties in Manchuria in 1935 (893.00 P.R. Mukden/99).

subfiles.title: Japanese Army Casualties in Manchuria, 1935
subfiles.about: A report records Japanese War Ministry figures for combat-related Army deaths in Manchukuo during 1935.
subfiles.summary: War Ministry announced 642 Army deaths in Manchukuo order-keeping in 1935, 140 more than 1934, from border incidents, bandit operations and Outer Mongolian incursions.
